competitors.name: Sortly
competitors.model: Freemium SaaS. Free = 100 unique items, 1 user, no label creation. Advanced $24/mo intro ($288/yr), regular $49/mo ($588/yr), 500 items, 2 seats. Ultra $74/mo intro ($888/yr), regular $149/mo ($1,788/yr), 2,000 items. Premium $149/mo intro, regular $299/mo ($3,588/yr), 5,000 items. Enterprise custom. Figures read directly off sortly.com/pricing, Aug 2026.
competitors.note: The name that shows up in every 'label your moving boxes with QR codes' article, and the App Store heavyweight at 4.73 from 9,432 US ratings. It is not a moving app — it is business inventory software that households wander into, and the pricing makes that obvious: QR label creation is gated to Advanced and above, so the exact thing a mover wants is the first thing behind the card. The soft spot is enormous and self-inflicted: the recent 1-star reviews are almost entirely a price-hike revolt ('Three years into the subscription they sent an email notification that the annual rate would increase by over 300% in 30 days (from $468 to $1428)'; 'my plan will jump to about $2,800 a year — more than double overnight'). One household reviewer put our whole pitch in a sentence: 'Great until you hit 100 items then have to pay $300 … crazy price for a household app.' A person moving house needs this tool for six weeks, once every seven years, and Sortly is architected to bill them forever.

competitors.name: Boxes: Storage made simple (StackTracks)
competitors.model: Freemium iOS/macOS app. Free tier widely reported by reviewers as 10 boxes / spaces / images ('Free version limits: 10 boxes/spaces/images'; 'you only get ten boxes and then everything from there costs money'). Paid unlock and a 'lifetime unlimited' IAP exist; StackTracks does not publish the figures on a public pricing page I could reach, so treat the exact prices as unverified.
competitors.note: This is the real feature bar and the app our redesign should be measured against, not Sortly. 4.84 from 939 US ratings, and its own store listing claims heavy/fragile/expensive/hazardous/temperature-sensitive flags, printing 'onto any label or paper size', 'print a manifest of your entire collection', NFC tags, custom attributes, exportable reports and shared team access. Its exploitable soft spots are all in the places software teams get lazy: the free cap is undisclosed until you hit it ('Add the limits of the free version. Please respect our time.'), the label printing is its worst-reviewed surface ('the label making process is a complete disaster … ended up buying 3 different Avery labels and they still would not print from the app correctly'), a redesign removed a label-size preset mid-move ('It was great until the update. I am in the middle of packing and now I have to enter all the details of a label'), and account conversion has eaten people's data ('changed my phone … it just deleted all my boxes with no way to recover + I paid'). Feature-complete, but the paper output — the part that actually goes on the box — is where it falls over.

competitors.name: Argosy QR (labels + companion app)
competitors.model: Physical product plus freemium app. ~$15 for a pack of 2" x 2" semi-gloss labels on Amazon (4.4 stars, ~175 reviews per the Yahoo smart-labels roundup); app free to scan up to 40 labels, then a paid subscription. App Store: 4.55 from 33 US ratings.
competitors.note: Veteran-owned, USA-made, and the one the lifestyle press keeps picking up — Apartment Therapy ran a hands-on review. The model is the razor-and-blades trap: you buy stickers, and the stickers are worthless without a subscription you did not price in. Its low reviews name every failure mode of a cloud-QR product at once — 'Photos Take Forever to Upload … over 5 minutes to load each one, even with a solid connection'; 'This app is extremely slow while you setup your labels … it just kept spinning'; and one buyer left with nothing: 'all the stickers came off the containers … I tried to open the app today and it wasn't working … Not worth the high annual cost of membership plus all the stickers I had to buy.' A five-star review even praises the vendor for fixing an *outage* within 24 hours — which quietly admits that a scanned label can return nothing at all. Every one of those failures is structurally impossible in a label whose payload is the label.

competitors.name: Smart Labels / SmartPacks (DHH Properties)
competitors.model: Physical sticker pack, ~$10 for 48 laminated 2" x 2.5" stickers; companion app free with no subscription (Yahoo smart-labels roundup: 4.6 stars from 375+ Amazon reviews; the iOS companion app is 4.91 from 2,453 US ratings).
competitors.note: The volume leader in the sticker aisle and the most credible of the label vendors — no subscription, unlimited photos, and by far the best App Store rating of anything in this category. Its App Store description is honest about what it is: 'This is the companion app for use with purchased Smart Labels.' That is the whole soft spot. The QR is a pre-printed serial that means nothing outside their app and their cloud, you cannot make more of them at 11pm when you run out, you cannot number a box #61 when the pack held 48, and a second person carrying the box has to install the app and be added to your account to read it. It also cannot be reprinted: our labels cost whatever a sheet of paper costs, theirs cost about 21 cents each and they are gone.

competitors.name: Everspruce Home Inventory
competitors.model: Freemium. Free tier stated on everspruceapp.com as up to 50 entries, with batch mode, photos, search, tags, CSV and PDF export, printed QR code labels, and up to 4 users. 'Plus' subscription for unlimited entries (price not stated on the pages I could read).
competitors.note: Positioned for insurance-grade home inventory but markets itself hard at movers, and it is the most generous free tier that still prints QR labels — CSV *and* PDF export free is genuinely better than most paid competitors. It is also the closest thing to an honest actor here and the hardest of this set to beat on features alone. Where we take it: 50 entries is a small move, the whole thing is account-and-cloud shaped, and its QR is still a pointer into Everspruce rather than the contents themselves. It is a home-inventory app that tolerates moving; nothing about the moving-day loop — labels on three sides, room signs, arrival reconciliation — is designed for.

competitors.name: Scanlily
competitors.model: Cloud SaaS with sold QR labels. Free = 1 user / 500 items. Pro $9/mo (2 users, 500 items). Ultra $35/mo (5 users, 2,000 items). Premium $75/mo (unlimited users, 5,000 items). Annual billing = 2 months free. 'Items with purchased Scanlily QR labels never count toward your item limit.' Figures from scanlily.com, Aug 2026.
competitors.note: The AI-forward entrant — photograph an item and it writes the description and category for you — and it is the one professional movers' blogs now name alongside Sortly. The item-limit exemption for purchased labels is a clever, ruthless mechanism: the free tier is deliberately generous right up to the point where buying their stickers becomes the cheapest way out. Soft spots: it is unambiguously cloud, account-gated and photo-upload-bound, which makes it useless in exactly the environment it will be used in — a house whose internet is not connected yet. And an AI that reads your possessions and stores them on someone else's server is a different privacy proposition from a notepad, whether or not the user can articulate why.

competitors.name: BoxOrganizer (BO24 UG, formerly Felix Moser)
competitors.model: Was free/one-off, now converting to subscription SaaS. Reviewers report the handover: 'The entire app has shifted to a software as a service which WILL push overpriced subscriptions. They're currently offering a free service but understand all of these apps end the same.'
competitors.note: Include this one not because it is a threat but because it is the category's cautionary tale, and it is fresh. It was the beloved indie QR box app — clean, cheap, offline-ish — and then it changed hands and the reviews collapsed into a wall of data loss: 'It wiped all of my data when I opened it back up after the update'; 'Lost all my info … I am very sad'; '5 Hours into organizing my room, I open the app and I've lost all my data with no way to get it back'; 'I chose this app extensively for moving. And now that I need it to find stuff it is no longer working and hangs.' It also now blocks you at a consent wall — 'The decline text does not do anything. You have to Allow to continue to use the app.' Its most-requested missing feature is the exact thing we already give away: 'My husband cannot use his own phone to scan what I've packed … your entire family needs to catalogue the same things on their own devices.'

competitors.name: A Sharpie, numbered boxes, and a note on your phone / a Google Sheet
competitors.note: The actual market leader and the thing every one of these apps loses to. It has no cap, no account, no login, works with a dead battery, and every professional mover's guide already teaches the method: number every box, write the destination room, keep a master list. Reviewers reach for it explicitly when an app disappoints — 'Deleted the app, I'll just make a note in my phone' and 'I could just use a notebook, spreadsheet, or qr scan labels.' It loses in exactly two places, and those two places are the whole reason our app should exist: it is not searchable when you are standing in a stack of 47 identical brown cubes, and it lives on one person's phone, so the mover holding the box and the partner in the other room cannot read it. Beat the Sharpie, not Sortly.

competitors.name: Free printable moving labels (Avery Design & Print, Etsy/TPT-style PDF packs, mover-branded colour-coded label kits)
competitors.model: Free templates from Avery; commercial colour-coded kits such as the ROOM ID system sell as physical packs of labels plus door signs; countless free printable PDF label sets from moving companies and organizing blogs.
competitors.note: This is what people actually print, and it is the design brief for our paper output. These kits ship the parts a screen app forgets: a colour per room, door signs for the new house so the crew can route boxes without asking, and a master colour key taped by the front door. HireAHelper's guide is explicit — put labels on 'at least two sides + the top' and 'Avoid marking the tops of boxes, as the labels will be hard to see when boxes are stacked in the moving truck.' They lose because paper is not searchable and cannot answer 'which box has the can opener.' Nobody currently ships both halves: the searchable database *and* the full printed kit. That gap is ours for the taking, and it is a print-stylesheet's worth of work, not a rewrite.

complaints.complaint: The inventory evaporates, and it evaporates precisely when you need it. 'My entire move disappeared all my photos my boxes and labels. And I can't get a answer as to what happened and how do I get it back' (Moving Boxes Pro, 1★). 'It wiped all of my data when I opened it back up after the update' and '5 Hours into organizing my room, I open the app and I've lost all my data with no way to get it back' (BoxOrganizer, 1★). 'I chose this app extensively for moving. And now that I need it to find stuff it is no longer working and hangs. I am speechless. Why did I pick this app?' (BoxOrganizer, 1★). 'Unlike other apps, you lose all of the move data if your phone needs to be replaced. I have 34 filled boxes and now have no idea what's in them' (Moving Organizer Lite, 1★).
complaints.source: Apple App Store US customer-review RSS feeds, fetched 9 Aug 2026: id 1265149542 (Moving Boxes Pro), id 1558366385 (BoxOrganizer), id 1113874641 (Moving Organizer Lite)
complaints.weWinIf: We already have JSON export/import in app.js, which puts us ahead of most of this field — but nobody exports a backup during a move, because 'when you're packing to move, you have minimal time to hassle with printing or remembering backups.' So make the backup automatic and physical: after the 10th box, and every 25 boxes after, a quiet inline row (never a modal, never over the thumb zone) that says how many boxes are unbacked-up and offers one tap to save the file. Add a human-readable CSV alongside the JSON, because a JSON file is not a backup to a normal person. And make the printed label itself the last-resort backup — the contents live inside the QR, so a printed sheet of labels is a full restore of the inventory even if the phone is at the bottom of a river.

complaints.complaint: The label is a pointer, so it dies when the company does — or just when the servers hiccup. Argosy's own five-star reviews praise them for fixing an outage 'within 24 hours', which means for 24 hours every QR label in the customer's garage pointed at nothing. Argosy 1★: 'I tried to open the app today and it wasn't working.'
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, id 1600403684 (Argosy QR); scanlily.com and sortly.com product architecture (all lookups are account-bound cloud records)
complaints.weWinIf: This is our entire strategic position and it should be stated on the label page in one sentence: the contents are inside the QR, not looked up from it. Prove it rather than claim it — a 'test this' line that tells the reader to turn off Wi-Fi and scan the label they just printed. Then add the mode that makes the promise absolute: a plain-text QR option, where the code carries the box number, room and contents as readable text with no URL at all, so any scanner on earth shows it with nothing loading, forever, including after Sky Wolf Studio stops existing.

complaints.complaint: The second person cannot read the labels. 'I love this app! But, it is a bit silly that you cannot share the data from your account. My husband cannot use his own phone to scan what I've packed to see what is in it and there is no way to share boxes, therefore … your entire family needs to catalogue the same things on their own devices. 🤦‍♀️ … I would pay a lifetime fee to have it.' (BoxOrganizer, 1★ for this reason alone.) Sortly gates a second seat at $24/mo; Scanlily gates it at $9/mo.
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, id 1558366385; sortly.com/pricing and scanlily.com pricing tables
complaints.weWinIf: We already win this and have never said so out loud. Because the box travels inside the link, a printed label is readable by the spouse, the teenager, the friend with the truck and the paid mover — on their own phone, with the camera app they already have, with no install, no account and no invitation. Put that on the page in the words of the complaint: 'anyone who can point a camera at the box can read it. They don't need the app, an account, or your permission.' It is the single most valuable sentence this app can print.

complaints.complaint: The free cap is hidden until you are already committed, mid-pack. 'Didn't realize I could only have one category until I was already three boxes into my packing session. If you're gonna limit people to how many categories they can have for free, at least say that up front. Very disappointed.' (Boxy, 2★.) 'Add the limits of the free version. Please respect our time. Free version limits: 10 boxes/spaces/images' (Boxes, 3★). 'Great until you hit 100 items then have to pay $300 … Wasted time loading in 100 items' (Sortly, 1★). Argosy meters at 40 labels; Scanlily at 500 items.
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, ids 6639614595 (Boxy), 1335784284 (Boxes), 529353551 (Sortly); scanlily.com pricing; local.yahoo.com smart-labels roundup for Argosy's 40-label free limit
complaints.weWinIf: Put the negative-space list exactly where every competitor puts its pricing table, and make each line a specific number they metered: no 10-box limit, no 100-item limit, no 40-label limit, no second-seat fee, no per-sticker cost, no subscription, no account. A person who just hit a wall somewhere else should be able to confirm in three seconds that there is no wall here. Also be honest about the one real ceiling we do have — app.js caps import at 500 boxes and 100 items per box — and say it up front rather than discovering it the way these reviewers did.

complaints.complaint: Typing every item is the abandonment point. 'So slow. Unless I missed something you need to manually type the name of everything you enter into the database when you enter it. This is so slow. Similar apps let you just take pictures of items as you throw them in a box. Then you can go back and label them later. That is a much better system.' (Boxes, 2★.) The whole current wave — BoxBuddy, BoxAeye, Scanlily — is built on removing typing, via photo-plus-AI or voice: 'Say what's going into the box while your hands are busy with tape and bubble wrap.'
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, id 1335784284; App Store listings for BoxBuddy (id 6758800955) and Scanlily's own site
complaints.weWinIf: We cannot ship cloud AI and should not want to, but we can beat everyone on the loop itself, because our entry surface is already a plain textarea — the fastest input control that exists. Target under ten seconds per box: keep focus in the textarea after sealing, default the room to the previous box's room (a person packs a kitchen, not a house), accept one-per-line or comma with no mode switch (already true in parseItems), and put a visible dictation hint on the field so people use the microphone their keyboard already has — free, offline, no API. Show the running count as feedback ('box 12 · 84 things') so the loop feels like progress rather than data entry.

complaints.complaint: Printing is the category's worst surface, and it fails at the moment of maximum stress. 'The app is great … the label making process is a complete disaster. The Avery labels are great but formatting the printer didn't work correctly, ended up buying 3 different Avery labels and they still would not print from the app correctly.' 'It was great until the update. I am in the middle of packing and now I have to enter all the details of a label that used to be in the system. If I could enter the Avery template number I wouldn't mind, but I have to manually put in all the measurements.' 'Needs a better way to print QR codes. I can't get air print to work. Like let me print them from my computer via a link or something.'
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, ids 1335784284 (Boxes, 3★ x2) and 1558366385 (BoxOrganizer, 3★)
complaints.weWinIf: This is the easiest big win available to us, because we are a web page and the competition is a phone app fighting AirPrint. We already print from a real computer to a real printer with no app in the way. Finish the job: a label-size choice (plain paper 2-up as now, plain paper 4-up, 2"x2" and 2"x4" Avery presets), a printed calibration square so a user can verify scale before wasting a sheet, a copies-per-box control, and a preview that shows the actual sheet. Say plainly on the page that it prints from any computer to any printer, on plain paper and tape if you have no labels.

complaints.complaint: Photos are treated as the point of the product, and every app under-delivers them. 'Useless without photos. And they take over 5 minutes to load each one, even with a solid connection' (Argosy, 1★). 'I wish they would allow access to photos or the ability to take more than one pic. You are only allowed to take one pic … So for now I try to spread everything on the ground and then take my ONE pic' (Moving Organizer Lite, 3★). 'the photo feature does not seem to be working for me … It's just giving me a greyed out icon' (Scan Your Boxes, 3★). 'Just wish I could sync between devices, print a list of contents, and add a picture of a box' (BoxOrganizer, 4★).
complaints.weWinIf: VERIFIED GAP: we have no photo capability at all. Add one photo per box, captured with a plain <input type="file" accept="image/*" capture="environment">, downscaled to roughly 800px and stored as a blob — local, instant, no upload, and therefore structurally faster than the market leader's five-minute wait. Note the storage consequence honestly and design for it: photos will not fit in localStorage at 40 boxes, so this is the feature that forces IndexedDB, and photos must be excluded from the QR payload and marked optional in the export. The pitch writes itself against Argosy's 1★: the photo appears the instant you take it, because it never goes anywhere.

complaints.complaint: Search finds the box but then stops. 'One suggestion — allow me to open and view box contents from the search' (Argosy, 4★). 'First would be a way to sort the boxes alphabetically. My naming system wasn't fully established when I made the first box and now it's hard to…' (Scan Your Boxes, 3★). 'It would be nice if you could group boxes by a group name. Also it would be nice to be able to download your inventory' (Argosy, 4★).
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, ids 1600403684 and 1471136904
complaints.weWinIf: VERIFIED GAP: our renderSearch() in app.js builds each result as a plain <li> with no click handler and silently truncates at 10 hits with no 'showing 10 of 23'. Make every result a button that scrolls to and highlights that box, show the true hit count, and let the box list group by room with per-room counts. The search box is the single reason this app exists on moving day and it currently ends in a dead end.

complaints.complaint: Do not write what is in the box on the outside of the box. Movers are unanimous: 'Avoid writing things like "jewelry" or "electronics" on the outside of boxes … Openly marking boxes with words like JEWELRY, VALUABLES, or CASH is an invitation to trouble. If you want your items to reach the right place but stay under the radar, use coded labels instead.' 'Writing "PlayStation" on a box makes it super tempting for someone to just grab it and run. "Family room" makes the box's contents less eye-catching.'
complaints.source: smithdray.com 'The Dos and Don'ts of Labeling Moving Boxes'; eastcoastwestcoastmovers.com moving-labels guide; safewise.com moving-security guide; corroborated by yahoo.com/qz.com 'How to prevent theft while you're moving'
complaints.weWinIf: VERIFIED CONFLICT IN OUR BUILD: renderLabels() prints the first four items of every box in plain text under the number, so a box containing a laptop advertises it to everyone who walks past. Flip the default — the printed label shows the box number huge, the room, and the QR, and nothing else — with an explicit opt-in toggle for 'print contents in plain text too.' Then market the QR as the security feature no competitor names: the label tells the mover where the box goes and tells nobody what is in it, and only someone holding the box can scan it.

complaints.complaint: One label per box is not how boxes are actually labelled. The professional convention is the 'Rule of Three' — 'Label the top and at least two adjacent sides of every box' — with a caveat: 'Avoid marking the tops of boxes, as the labels will be hard to see when boxes are stacked in the moving truck.' Movers also expect a colour per room, a master colour key 'in a visible spot, such as near the front door', door signs at the destination, FRAGILE in bold contrasting text, orientation arrows, an 'OPEN FIRST' essentials box, and weight estimates. And: 'Don't forget to explain your system to helpers or hired movers.'
complaints.source: olympiamoving.com 'Labeling Moving Boxes: Do's, Don'ts & Smart Strategies'; hireahelper.com 'How to Color-Code Boxes for Moving'; corroborated by carrollsmv.com and the ROOM ID commercial kit sold on teamboxops.com
complaints.weWinIf: VERIFIED GAP: renderLabels() emits exactly one label per box, with no room colour, no handling flags and no room signage. Ship the whole printed kit in one 'Print the move' action: three identical labels per box, a per-room door sign at A4/Letter with the room name and its colour, and a one-page master key listing each room, its colour and its box count. That is a print-stylesheet's worth of work and it is the thing every commercial label kit sells for $25 and no app prints at all.

complaints.complaint: The fear is not disorganisation, it is the box that never arrives. Reviewers describe standing in the new place unable to answer basic questions — 'I have 34 filled boxes and now have no idea what's in them' — and the moving-industry guidance around numbered labels exists specifically so you can reconcile against 'a digital manifest' when the truck is unloaded. None of the consumer apps surfaced in this research ships an arrival check.
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, id 1113874641 (Moving Organizer Lite, 1★); olympiamoving.com labeling guide ('Use numbered labels for high-volume moves with a digital manifest')
complaints.weWinIf: VERIFIED GAP: our box model in app.js is {id, n, room, items} — there is no status field anywhere. Add a single status per box (packed → loaded → arrived) driven by one giant tap target per box, plus a headline reconciliation readout: '34 of 47 arrived · missing: 12, 19, 33.' It is the one screen a person will hold up in front of a moving crew, so it must be legible at arm's length in daylight, and it is the emotional payoff of having numbered anything in the first place.

complaints.complaint: Consent walls and tracking in a free utility. 'First time opening the app in a while and it goes to a page that explains the app's data use policy, then some underlined text "No, I do not want to contribute to improving the app" and a button on the bottom of the screen to "Allow Analytics". The decline text does not do anything. You have to Allow to continue to use the app. Why even put the text to decline if you won't let people choose it.' Separately, of a redesigned competitor: 'not only do they want me to pay for using the app, they want to spy/track what I…'
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, ids 1558366385 (BoxOrganizer, 1★) and 1335784284 (Boxes, 1★)
complaints.weWinIf: Say the negative claim in plain words rather than as a privacy assurance: there is no analytics in this page, no cookie banner, no consent dialog, because there is nothing to consent to. Reinforce it with a fact the user can check: the box contents ride in the part of the link after the # — and the fragment is never sent to a web server, by design of the web itself. That is a verifiable technical claim, not a promise, and it is exactly the kind of falsifiable statement the portfolio brief says people actually believe.

complaints.complaint: Deleting is one tap and permanent, and this is a category where people work at midnight while exhausted. Across these apps every complaint about lost work is about irreversibility, and no reviewed competitor mentions an undo. Sortly reviewers report the softer version — 'It either doesn't save or looses data. It freezes the entire iPad.'
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, id 529353551 (Sortly, 1★); pattern inferred across ids 1558366385, 1335784284, 1265149542 — no competitor undo was observed in any listing or review, so read the absence as unverified rather than proven
complaints.weWinIf: VERIFIED GAP: app.js deletes a box behind a native window.confirm() and then filters it out of the array permanently. Replace the blocking browser dialog with an immediate delete plus an undo affordance in the existing toast (we already have a toast with role=status), and keep the last few deletions recoverable for the session. The native confirm() is also the wrong control here — it is unstyleable, it blocks the page, and on a phone it lands under the thumb, which is precisely the mis-tap pattern the portfolio brief bans.

complaints.complaint: Exports that are not readable by a human, or that do not exist. 'The only missing part is sharing the data with others, or some external sources: PDF, Excel, etc … without the option to export the data and being able to access it from another source, in case the app stops working with an iOS upgrade, is a must. I have to pack more then 5,000 items in probably 300 boxes, and I can't imagine investing such amount of time without a secure way to access…' Another: 'Y'all really need to make it where it backs up / and have the ability to share. If for whatever reason you delete the app or otherwise ALL DATA IS GONE!' Everspruce ships CSV and PDF export on its free tier.
complaints.source: Apple App Store US review RSS, id 1558366385 (BoxOrganizer, 5★ and 1★); everspruceapp.com free-tier feature list
complaints.weWinIf: PARTIAL GAP: exportBtn writes moving-boxes.json and nothing else. Add CSV (box, room, status, contents) so it opens in Sheets or Excel, and treat the printed manifest as the PDF export — 'Print → Save as PDF' is a free PDF exporter every browser already has, and saying so on the page turns a missing feature into an existing one.

tableStakes: Scanning a printed label shows that box's contents. BROKEN IN OUR BUILD, and it is the headline feature. /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps/moving-boxes/index.html has `<main id="main">` at line 1248 wrapping `<div id="main">` at line 1259 — the only duplicate element id in the entire 23-app portfolio (checked across all apps/*/index.html). /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps/moving-boxes/app.js showScanned() calls `$('main').classList.add('hidden')`, and document.getElementById returns the first match in tree order, which is the outer <main> — the ancestor of #reveal. With `.hidden{display:none !important}`, unhiding #reveal inside a hidden <main> does nothing: a scanned QR renders a page with a header, a footer and no box. Fix before any redesign work; then add a regression test, because helpers.test.mjs currently only covers the pure functions and would never have caught this.

A photo of the open box. MISSING ENTIRELY. index.html has exactly four inputs — boxNum, boxRoom, boxItems and the hidden importFile — and the box model in app.js is {id, n, room, items}. Every competitor has photos, the current wave (BoxBuddy, BoxAeye, Scanlily) is built around them, and 'Useless without photos' is a literal 1★ on Argosy. Local capture with no upload is also our fastest possible answer to their slowest feature.

Tapping a search result opens the box. MISSING. renderSearch() in app.js builds each hit as an <li> with no click handler, no keyboard affordance and a hard `.slice(0, 10)` with no indication that results were truncated. Search is the entire moving-day use case and it currently dead-ends.

Undo for a deleted box. MISSING. app.js uses `confirm('Delete box #N?')` then permanently filters the array. A blocking native dialog under the thumb is the exact mis-tap pattern the portfolio brief forbids, and the loss is unrecoverable.

Box status and an arrival reconciliation count. MISSING. No status field exists in the model. Numbering boxes is pointless if the app cannot answer 'did all 47 arrive?' — the question the whole system is built to answer, and the one moment of genuine fear in a move.

Handling flags on the label: FRAGILE, THIS WAY UP, HEAVY, OPEN FIRST. MISSING from both the model and renderLabels(). Competitor 'Boxes' advertises heavy/fragile/expensive/hazardous/temperature-sensitive as a headline feature; every professional labelling guide lists them; ours prints none.

Room as a first-class, colour-coded, countable thing. MISSING. Room is free text with a datalist of previously-used values; renderBoxes() sorts by number only, with no grouping, no per-room counts and no colour. Colour-per-room plus a master key by the front door is the single strongest convention in this category and the thing the commercial label kits actually sell.

Print controls: label size, sheet layout, and more than one label per box. MISSING. The print rules in index.html hard-code a two-column grid with a 6mm gap and a 30mm QR; there is no page-size option, no Avery preset, no calibration mark and no copies-per-box control, so the professional 'label two sides and the top' rule is impossible. Competitor 'Boxes' claims printing 'onto any label or paper size' and still gets 3★ reviews for it — this surface is winnable and we are currently below the floor.

A deliberate printed manifest. ACCIDENTAL, NOT DESIGNED. The Boxes card in index.html is not marked .screenonly, so hitting Print emits the whole box list ahead of the labels — untitled, unstyled, and unavoidable. There is no way to print labels without it or it without labels, and the heading reads '12 boxes · 84 things' rather than anything a mover could use. Turn the accident into the product: a proper one-page manifest with room totals is what the industry guidance means by 'a digital manifest'.

Export a human can read. PARTIAL. exportBtn produces moving-boxes.json only. Everspruce gives CSV and PDF away on its free tier; a JSON file is not a backup to the person who most needs one. Add CSV, and name 'Print → Save as PDF' as the PDF path.

A QR that actually scans at the size we print it. AT RISK — arithmetic, not opinion. encodeBoxForLabel() caps the payload at 900 base64 characters, which lands around QR version 21 (101 modules) plus a 4-module quiet zone each side; printed at the hard-coded 30mm that is roughly 0.27mm per module, at the bottom edge of the ~0.25mm absolute floor print-QR guides cite and well under the working minimum once home-printer dot gain and a phone camera in bad light are involved. A ten-item box is fine (~0.43mm/module); a heavily packed kitchen box is not. Either raise the printed size for dense codes, drop the payload cap well below 900, or shorten the encoding — and test a worst-case label on an actual inkjet before shipping.

Works offline, installs, needs no account, keeps data on the device. PRESENT AND AHEAD OF THE FIELD — sw.js (cache 'boxes-v10') precaches every asset, manifest.webmanifest is a valid installable PWA, storage is localStorage with a full-storage warning toast, and export/import exists. Every paid competitor in this set is cloud-and-account bound. This is already true; the gap is that the page barely says it.
differentiators: The label IS the database. Every competitor's QR is a foreign key into an account on their server; ours carries the box number, room and contents inside the code. Lead with it in the words the reviews use: no app to install, no account, no signal, nothing to expire — 'scan it with the mover's phone, in a house whose internet isn't connected yet, in ten years.' It is the direct answer to 'My entire move disappeared', to a competitor's 24-hour outage, and to 'my husband cannot use his own phone to scan what I've packed.' No company with a server can copy it, because their server is their business model.

Ship a plain-text QR mode and make the promise absolute. A URL still needs a page to load; a text QR needs nothing at all. Offer a per-print choice — 'link (opens a tidy page)' or 'plain text (any scanner, zero network, forever)' — and explain the trade in one line each. This is the only version of this product that still works after we are gone, and being the app that plans for its own death is a trust argument nobody else in this category can make.

State the privacy claim as a checkable fact, not a value. The contents ride after the # in the link, and URL fragments are never transmitted to a web server — that is how the web works, not a policy we promise. Pair it with 'no analytics, no cookie banner, no consent dialog, because there is nothing to consent to', aimed squarely at the competitor whose decline button does not work.

Print the entire moving kit, not stickers. One 'Print the move' action producing three identical labels per box (the movers' Rule of Three), a per-room door sign for the new house, and a one-page master key with each room's colour and box count. Commercial kits sell exactly this bundle as a physical product; every app ships only the stickers. We are a web page talking to a real printer, which is the one surface where a phone app cannot follow us.

The discreet label, marketed as a security feature. Number huge, room, QR — and nothing about what's inside — because every mover's guide says writing 'electronics' on a box is an invitation. Contents stay behind a code only the person holding the box can read. Nobody in this category has noticed that their QR is a privacy feature; it is free positioning sitting on the table.

Moving-day mode: the arrival count. One screen, enormous type, '34 of 47 arrived — missing: 12, 19, 33', tappable at arm's length while a crew carries boxes past. Numbering exists to make this question answerable and not one consumer competitor answers it. It is also the emotional peak of the product and therefore the moment worth designing hardest.

Publish the negative-space list where the others put a pricing table, with their real numbers in it: no 10-box cap (Boxes), no 100-item cap (Sortly), no 40-label cap (Argosy), no 500-item cap (Scanlily), no $24/mo second seat, no 21-cents-a-sticker, no subscription, no account, no upload wait. Every line answers a sourced complaint, costs us nothing, and is structurally uncopyable by anyone paying for servers.

Win the packing loop on seconds per box. A plain textarea is already the fastest input control that exists; make the rest of the loop match — focus stays put after sealing, the room defaults to the previous box's room, one-per-line or commas with no mode switch, a visible dictation hint so people use the free offline microphone their keyboard already has, and a running count as the feedback. The category's documented abandonment point is typing; we beat AI capture not with AI but by never making the user leave the field.

Be the best-looking thing in a category of clip-art moving trucks. The competition is either enterprise-blue inventory dashboards or App Store-generic sticker companions, and the free alternative is a Sharpie. A confident, industrial, high-contrast design that looks like shipping and warehousing — not like a moving company's brochure — is a differentiator on its own, and it is the one the tip jar depends on.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: Two visual camps, both beatable. Camp one is the sticker-pack companion app — Argosy, Smart Labels/SmartPacks, ToteScan, Smatagee — whose identity is the rainbow of the stickers themselves: bright multicoloured 2" squares, rounded photo cards, a big scan button, and otherwise a stock iOS look. Camp two is inventory SaaS — Sortly, Scanlily, BoxHero — which is enterprise blue-and-white dashboard: folder trees, custom fields, tables, reports, and an upgrade banner. Around both sits the moving industry itself, which is overwhelmingly orange: U-Haul, PODS, Home Depot boxes, Budget, plus kraft brown and the red-and-black of FRAGILE and THIS WAY UP tape. Dated tells to avoid outright: skeuomorphic 3D cardboard-box illustrations with a strip of tape across the flap, wood-grain or corrugation textures used as decoration, moving-truck clip art, a couple in a bare living room holding a box and laughing, drop shadows on everything, gradient buttons, friendly rounded fonts trying to make a stressful week feel jolly, and the hamburger-menu-then-dashboard structure that hides the search bar. What reads as current in 2026: the working surface on the first screen with no marketing preamble, search as the home screen rather than a feature, capture-first entry (photo or voice) treated as the default path, flat near-monochrome surfaces with a single accent used for state rather than decoration, generous tap targets, real dark mode, and — the sharpest signal of all right now, because the AI wave made everyone cloud-bound — offline and local-first stated proudly as a feature rather than buried as an implementation detail.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: Three different people open this app, and only one of them chose it. FIRST, the packer: three weeks out, 9pm, standing over an open box in a half-dismantled room with a marker in one hand, dust on their fingers and tape on their sleeve, about to repeat the same interaction forty to eighty times. Every second of friction is multiplied by the box count, so the entry loop is the whole design; this is also the person who quits at box ten if it feels like data entry, which is the documented failure of the category. SECOND, the same person on moving day or the week after: in a bare room with no furniture and no internet connected, phone at 12%, standing in a wall of identical brown cubes, needing to know which one has the kettle, the shower curtain, the bolts for the bed frame, or the passports — and quietly terrified that one box is not there. Moving reliably ranks among the most stressful things people do, and it usually arrives bundled with a job change, a separation, a new baby or a death, so the register must be steady and competent, never chirpy. THIRD, and the one nobody designs for: a helper or a paid mover holding a box in a doorway, who has installed nothing and agreed to nothing, needing to know in under two seconds which room this goes in. That third user dictates more than the other two combined: no account, no install, no login, and a box number and room legible from two metres in daylight. Practically, all of it means: the entry field is the first thing on screen and keeps focus; the box number is the largest object on both screen and paper; search returns a tappable answer, not a list; every destructive action is recoverable, because 'delete box 34' happens at midnight; contrast is high enough for a bright empty room and a dim garage; nothing animates, grows or moves under the thumb; and the printed artifact has to survive packing tape, a rainy driveway, a box knife and a black-and-white laser printer.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: sturdy, industrial, plainspoken, high-contrast, unfussy, quick

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Stay in the kraft/dun family the app already owns (hue ~66–72) but change what kind of colour it is: drop the chroma from 0.105 to roughly 0.05 and drop the accent's value hard, from the current mid-tone caramel #a87632 to a dark stencil-ink umber in the #3a2c18–#4a3a22 range (target L≈0.30–0.34, C≈0.05). Deepen the canvas from stationery cream #fef6ea to a corrugated tone around #f2e6d2, and keep card surfaces near-white so they read as shipping labels lying on cardboard. Then reserve saturation for two jobs only: a fixed eight-swatch room palette (the one place colour carries meaning) and the existing warm red #b63d28 used exclusively for exceptions — fragile, missing, unaccounted-for. Change the texture from `grid` to `band`, and treat the band as a strip of packing tape rather than graph paper.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Three forces, and unusually they all point the same way. (1) CATEGORY: the moving industry is orange — U-Haul, PODS, Budget, Home Depot's box aisle — and the label aisle is a rainbow of sticker colours. Both are unavailable to us for the same reason red is unavailable to a PDF tool: adopting the category's colour in a category full of near-identical apps reads as one more of them. Kraft brown is the honest alternative and it is already ours; the problem is not the hue. (2) PORTFOLIO, read from /workspaces/SWS-apps/design/skins.mjs: moving-boxes currently sits at hue 72 / chroma 0.105 / warm paper / technical voice / grid texture. signup-sheets is hue 58, warm, technical — fourteen degrees away with the same paper and the same voice. sitter-sheet is 86, warm. specials-planner is 38, warm. Worse, home-inventory — explicitly the sibling app — is hue 124, chroma 0.085, warm, technical, grid: the same recipe on all four non-hue axes, separated only by 52°. We are the most crowded slot in the studio and hue alone cannot fix it, so the differentiation has to come from value and chroma. Every warm app in the portfolio uses a mid-value accent around L 0.5 on a near-white cream; being the one warm app with a near-black accent on a visibly darker ground separates it at a glance, from across a room, in a way another 15° of hue never would. (3) FUNCTION, which is decisive: this is the only app in the portfolio that needs a categorical palette, because colour-per-room is the strongest convention in the category and the thing the commercial label kits actually sell. A categorical palette only works if the brand gets out of its way — a caramel brand accent will fight a 'Kitchen = amber' chip and lose. Near-achromatic brand, saturated data: the same argument caregiver-log (chroma 0.035) and signature-maker (chroma 0.022) already make, and this app can make it without colliding with either, since both are editorial-voiced grain-textured apps in different hue families. There is a second functional payoff: the printed label is black on white and most people print in mono, so a near-black brand accent means the screen and the paper finally look like the same product. And the deeper corrugated canvas is not decoration — it gives the white label cards somewhere to sit, which is exactly the figure/ground problem a labelling app has.
colorRecommendation.avoid: U-Haul/PODS/Home Depot orange (#F7941D, #F96302 and neighbours) — it is the category's colour and adopting it makes a free indie tool look like a moving company's lead-gen app. The current mid-value caramel #a87632/#8e5d11 as the primary accent — it is the same value band as signup-sheets' marigold, specials-planner's terracotta and sitter-sheet's honey, all of which also sit on cream, and at 14–34° of hue separation value is the only axis left that can do the work. The `grid` texture — home-inventory, qr-maker and scan-to-pdf already use it, and on the app with the most crowded hue slot it is the wrong axis to share; corrugation or a tape band says 'box' without saying 'graph paper'. Any brand colour with enough chroma to compete with a room chip; if a user cannot tell 'this is the Kitchen colour' from 'this is the app's colour' in half a second, the room palette is dead. Rainbow sticker-colour UI — that is camp one's whole look and it is indistinguishable across five vendors. Wood-grain, corrugated-cardboard photo textures, tape-strip drop shadows and any 3D box illustration — the defining dated tell of the moving category. Green as a status colour on its own for 'arrived' — pair it with a checkmark and the box number, because this screen gets read across a room by someone who is not the owner and may well be colour-blind. And never let colour alone carry FRAGILE or an exception state on the printed label, since most people print in black and white and every colour cue vanishes on the way to the paper.

confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH overall, with the highest confidence on the parts that matter most and named gaps elsewhere. HIGHEST CONFIDENCE — OUR OWN BUILD: everything asserted about /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps/moving-boxes/ was read directly from index.html, app.js, helpers.js, sw.js and manifest.webmanifest on 9 Aug 2026. The duplicate `id="main"` (index.html lines 1248 and 1259) is verified fact, and I confirmed by grep across all 23 apps/*/index.html that moving-boxes is the only app with a duplicated id. The consequence — showScanned() hiding the ancestor of #reveal via getElementById tree-order resolution — is a code reading, not a runtime test: no browser or jsdom was available in this environment, so I could not execute the scan path. Someone should open a printed-label URL in a browser to confirm before the fix is scoped, though the CSS (`.hidden{display:none !important}`) leaves little room for doubt. Note also that index.html was regenerated by the design build at 14:58 during this session, so line numbers may drift; the pattern will not. HIGH CONFIDENCE — REVIEWS: all quoted user reviews come from Apple's public US customer-review RSS feeds, fetched directly (itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/...) for app ids 529353551 Sortly, 1335784284 Boxes, 1558366385 BoxOrganizer, 1265149542 Moving Boxes Pro, 1600403684 Argosy QR, 1113874641 Moving Organizer Lite, 1471136904 Scan Your Boxes, 6639614595 Boxy. These are verbatim; no quote in this document was paraphrased or invented. CAVEAT: the RSS feed returns only a recent window (roughly 50 reviews per app, and for some apps only one page returned content), so this is a recency sample, not a representative one, and it skews toward whoever wrote last. Ratings and rating counts come from the iTunes lookup API the same day. HIGH CONFIDENCE — PRICING: Sortly's tiers, item caps and the fact that QR label creation starts at Advanced were read off sortly.com/pricing directly; Scanlily's tiers and the 'purchased labels never count toward your item limit' clause off scanlily.com directly. MEDIUM CONFIDENCE: the Boxes app's free cap of 10 boxes is user-reported in two separate App Store reviews, not from StackTracks — I could not reach a published pricing page, and the 'lifetime unlimited' price is unverified. Argosy's $15 label price, its 40-label free scan limit, SmartPacks at $10/48 stickers and ToteScan/Smatagee figures all come from a single Yahoo smart-labels roundup (local.yahoo.com), a commerce article with affiliate incentives — directionally reliable, but I would not quote the prices publicly without checking Amazon. Everspruce's 50-entry free tier and free CSV/PDF export come from everspruceapp.com's own marketing pages; the Plus price is unstated. NOT VERIFIED: Reddit. Every search that should have surfaced r/moving threads returned commerce pages and App Store listings instead, and a DuckDuckGo Lite fallback returned no results, so there is zero first-hand community sentiment in this document — if you want the richest gripe texture, someone should read r/moving and r/organization manually. Apartment Therapy's Argosy hands-on returned HTTP 403 and Google Play review pages truncated on fetch, so Android sentiment is absent entirely. NOT VERIFIED — COMPETITOR UNDO: I found no competitor that ships undo, but absence of evidence in a review sample is not evidence of absence; treat that table-stakes line as 'we lack it' rather than 'they lack it too'. ARITHMETIC, NOT MEASUREMENT: the QR scannability warning is computed from the 900-character cap in helpers.js against standard QR byte capacities and the 30mm print width in index.html, cross-checked against published minimum-module-size guidance (scanova.io and similar print-QR guides cite a ~0.25mm module floor and a 2cm minimum overall). Nobody printed and scanned a worst-case label. That test is cheap and should be run before the redesign commits to a label size. PORTFOLIO PALETTE: read from design/skins.mjs directly and from the generated tokens at the top of moving-boxes/index.html, so the hue/chroma/paper/voice/texture collisions cited are exact, not sampled.
